name: MS Office 2016 - SheetProtection
aliases: OOXML sheetProtection hashValue; Excel sheet protection password (SHA-512); Office 2013+ protection verifier
notes:
WHERE THE HASH LIVES. This is not document encryption and office2john does
not extract it. An .xlsx is a zip; the digest is a cleartext attribute run
on the protection element of the relevant part:

    <sheetProtection algorithmName="SHA-512" hashValue="..."
                     saltValue="..." spinCount="100000" sheet="1"/>

THE ATTRIBUTE NAMES ARE NOT UNIFORM, which is where a naive extractor goes
wrong. `<sheetProtection>`, `<chartsheetProtection>` and `<fileSharing>` use
the bare names above. `<workbookProtection>` carries TWO INDEPENDENT digests
under PREFIXED names: workbookAlgorithmName / workbookHashValue /
workbookSaltValue / workbookSpinCount for the structure password, and
revisionsAlgorithmName / revisionsHashValue / revisionsSaltValue /
revisionsSpinCount for the revisions password. Word's
`<w:documentProtection>`, `<w:writeProtection>` and `<w:modifyVerifier>` use
the bare names again, namespace-prefixed.

Measured 2026-09-03: sheetProtection, fileSharing and BOTH prefixed
workbookProtection slots round-trip at mode 25300, against fixtures whose
attribute spellings come from openpyxl's own schema classes rather than from
recollection. The Word elements were exercised only against a hand-written
.docx, so those spellings remain spec reading and not measurement.

THE HASHCAT LINE is built from three of those attributes and two literals:

    $office$2016$0$<spinCount>$<saltValue>$<hashValue>

`2016` and `0` never vary; salt precedes hash; both go in base64 exactly as
the XML spells them. Getting the order wrong or using ':' as the separator
produces hashcat's "separator unmatched", which reads like a corrupt hash
rather than a malformed line.

HASHCAT'S PARSER IS STRICTER THAN THE FILE FORMAT, and its error names the
wrong field. src/modules/module_25300.c in v7.1.2-549 requires the spinCount
token to be six digits AND to equal 100000 (line 165), the salt to be
exactly 24 base64 characters decoding to 16 bytes, and the digest exactly 88
decoding to 64. Probed against the binary across ten spin values on
2026-09-03: only 100000 loads, and every other value is rejected as
"Salt-value exception", which sends the reader off to inspect the salt.
Excel's own default is 100000 so most real files pass, but a document
written with any other spin count has a real, well-formed SHA-512 digest and
NO hashcat mode at all.

THE CONSTRUCTION, measured 2026-09-03 by reproducing hashcat's own example
vector above with all four plausible orderings and finding exactly one
match:

    H_0 = SHA512(saltValue . utf16le(password))
    H_i = SHA512(H_{i-1} . uint32le(i-1))   for i = 1 .. spinCount
    hashValue = base64(H_spinCount)

The counter is APPENDED and 0-BASED. Agile ENCRYPTION prepends it, and that
difference is the whole trap: the prepending order computes a perfectly
well-formed digest that simply is not this one, with nothing to indicate the
error. It is SHA-512 throughout, not SHA-256; secondary write-ups say SHA-256
and are wrong. hashcat's 25300 kernel is SHA-512 only, so a file whose
algorithmName is anything else has no mode.

Proven end to end on 2026-09-03 against a synthesized .xlsx carrying a
SHA-512 sheetProtection element for a known password, extracted from the
XML and cracked by hashcat at this mode.

The pre-2013 form of the same feature is a 16-bit verifier in a `password`
attribute, which is a different algorithm and has its own entry:
ms-office-sheetprotection-legacy. And for either form, note that the file is
not encrypted -- deleting the protection element and rezipping opens the
sheet, so cracking is only warranted when the password itself is the object.

name: MS Office SheetProtection - legacy 16-bit verifier
aliases: Excel sheet protection password; Excel workbook protection password; sheetProtection password attribute; BIFF Password/Protect record; Binary Document Password Verifier Derivation Method 1
denotation: Binary Document Password Verifier Derivation Method 1
application: Microsoft Excel <=2010 file format; still written by openpyxl and by LibreOffice
notes:
A 16-bit password verifier, not a hash in any useful sense. In an OOXML part
it appears under a DIFFERENT ATTRIBUTE NAME on each element: `password` on
`<sheetProtection>` and `<chartsheetProtection>`, `workbookPassword` and
`revisionsPassword` on `<workbookProtection>` (two independent passwords on
one element), and `reservationPassword` on `<fileSharing>`. Spellings taken
from openpyxl's schema classes and exercised 2026-09-03. It is also the data
of the BIFF PASSWORD and PROTECT records in a pre-2007 .xls. The native form
-- the one the vector
above is written in -- is FOUR HEXADECIMAL DIGITS exactly as the attribute
spells them, with no wrapper, no salt and no iteration count, because there
is nowhere for any of those to go.

The algorithm, from MS-OFFCRYPTO 2.3.7.1: start at 0; for each character of
the password taken from LAST to FIRST, rotate the running value left within
15 bits and xor the character code; then rotate once more, xor the password
length, and xor the constant 0xCE4B. Reimplemented and measured 2026-09-03
against the value openpyxl 3.0.9 writes for "P@ssw0rd", which is the vector
above.

BYTE ORDER IS A TRAP. The XML attribute and the BIFF record render the same
word in opposite orders, so published write-ups give "AB94" for the value
this repository records as "94AB". They are the same verifier. Check which
container a quoted value came out of before comparing it to anything.

THE ORIGINAL PASSWORD IS NOT RECOVERABLE and no tool will ever make it so:
16 bits cannot carry it. What is recoverable is a COLLIDING password, which
unlocks the sheet just as well. Measured 2026-09-03: 'DbOUJLIb' verifies to
94AB, found in 24065 random 8-character tries in under a second. Do not
report such a string as the password.

Collisions are dense but NOT uniformly reachable, which is the practical
gotcha. Exhausting printable ASCII at lengths 1 to 4 -- 82,317,120 strings
-- reaches only 1536 distinct verifier values out of 65536, and 94AB is not
among them, because a short password is rotated too few times for the high
bits ever to be set. Search at the same length as the original or longer; a
short-candidate sweep can return nothing and prove nothing.

Operationally, cracking is usually the wrong move for either form of sheet
protection. The file is not encrypted: deleting the protection element and
rezipping opens the sheet, and only a genuine interest in the password
itself (credential reuse, an investigation) justifies the rest.
